opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a big part of it was the feedback loop. In RL research back then, you'd come up with an idea, implement it, and then wait hours or even days for experiments to finish. And when the results came back, you often couldn't tell whether your idea didn't work or whether you just had a bug somewhere, or a bad hyperparameter, or an unlucky random seed. The variance was huge. You could run the same algorithm with five seeds and get five very different curves.

So a lot of my time wasn't really spent thinking about interesting questions. It was spent debugging infrastructure, tuning things, and rerunning experiments. That's part of why I got into building tools. I felt that if the frameworks and environments were faster and cleaner, at least the engineering pain would go down and people could focus on the actual ideas.

There was also a mismatch between what got rewarded and what I thought mattered. Many papers were about squeezing out a few more points on Atari or MuJoCo benchmarks, and it wasn't always clear that those improvements were real or would transfer to anything useful. When you're a student, you start asking yourself, "Am I solving a real problem, or just optimizing a leaderboard?" That made it hard for me to feel the work was meaningful.

What I did enjoy was the engineering side: making things run ten times faster, making a library that other people could actually use. That gave me a much more direct sense of impact. Looking back, it pushed me toward working on systems and infrastructure, and later on applying RL in settings like large language models, where it finally felt like it was solving something real.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a lot of it came down to how brittle everything felt. When I was working on RL, you'd set up an experiment, and the result would depend so heavily on things that had nothing to do with the idea you were actually testing. Change the random seed, and the agent learns in one run and completely fails in the next. Tweak one hyperparameter slightly, and the whole curve shifts. So you'd spend most of your time not thinking about the research question, but babysitting training runs and trying to figure out whether a result was real or just noise.

That was frustrating for me, because I like building things that work reliably. When I was writing Tianshou, the part I enjoyed was the engineering: making the library clean, making it fast, making it so other people could actually reproduce results. The research side, where you had to convince yourself and reviewers that a small gain over a baseline was meaningful, felt a lot less satisfying. You'd see papers where the improvement was within the variance across seeds, and everyone kind of knew it, but the incentive was to publish anyway.

The other thing was the gap between the simulated environments and anything real. We were spending enormous effort getting an agent to do slightly better on Atari or MuJoCo, and it was hard to see how that connected to problems people actually cared about. It felt like a very closed loop. Compared with that, working on infrastructure or on systems where you get a clear signal that something is useful, that felt much more rewarding to me at the time.

I don't think RL itself is bad, to be clear. It's just that the day-to-day experience of doing RL research back then, with the noise, the compute cost, and the weak connection to real applications, didn't match what I found enjoyable about doing technical work.
